Five Ways This Curriculum Prepared You for What's Coming

A Gartner forecast suggests 33% of enterprise software will include agentic AI by 2028—a pace that, if it holds, implies something worth examining about where PMM skills need to go.

By Chris O'Hara · 8 min read

A stat landed last week that deserves more attention than it's getting. Gartner predicts that 33% of enterprise software will include agentic AI by 2028—up from less than 1% in 2024—and that 15% of day-to-day work decisions will be made autonomously. Not AI-assisted or AI-recommended, but autonomous in a way that changes the relationship between the marketer and the tools they use.

33%
of enterprise software will include agentic AI by 2028
— Gartner, August 2026

The implications are worth thinking through. The CRM systems, marketing automation platforms, and ERP tools that product marketers interact with every day are all moving toward embedded agent capabilities—not as features you summon when you need help, but as persistent collaborators that analyze data, surface recommendations, and execute tasks on their own initiative. The question isn't whether this transition is happening; the evidence suggests it's already underway. The question is whether product marketers have the right foundation to work effectively in that environment.

If you've been working through this curriculum, there's reason to think you do—even if that wasn't immediately obvious as the goal.

What Most AI Training Gets Wrong

The typical approach to "AI for marketers" focuses on tool usage—prompt engineering, ChatGPT techniques, ways to make language models write your emails faster. That knowledge has value, but it addresses the surface layer of a deeper architectural shift. The more consequential change isn't AI as a tool you invoke; it's AI as a layer that permeates the software environment, making decisions on your behalf, communicating with other agents, and operating continuously whether you're paying attention or not.

Working effectively in that environment requires something different from prompt skills. It requires an understanding of how to architect systems in which AI operates—how to structure data so agents can use it, how to define boundaries and governance, how to maintain quality when automation handles the routine work. That architectural perspective is what this curriculum has been building toward, often implicitly.

Five Capabilities Worth Noting

1. Building Content for Two Audiences

Unit 2 introduced the concept of Generative Engine Optimization—the recognition that content now serves two distinct audiences. Human buyers remain the ultimate decision-makers, but AI systems increasingly mediate what those humans see and consider. When recent research suggests that 72% of holiday shoppers now consult ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini for product recommendations, the implication is clear: positioning, messaging, and competitive differentiation all need to be legible to machines, structured in ways that AI systems can parse and surface accurately.

This dual-audience thinking hasn't yet penetrated most PMM practice. The curriculum introduced it early.

2. Personas Structured for Agent Consumption

Unit 10 addressed a persistent weakness in B2B marketing: personas assembled from assumptions and workshop exercises rather than observable behavior. The traditional persona—a PDF that lives in SharePoint and rarely influences actual decisions—has limited value in any context, but it has essentially no value to an agentic system that needs structured, behavioral data to make decisions about account prioritization or message selection.

The persona frameworks introduced in Unit 10 emphasize behavioral signals over hypothetical preferences, and they're structured in ways that AI systems can operationalize. That's not incidental to the agentic future; it's central to it.

3. Competitive Intelligence at Continuous Speed

Competitive intelligence has traditionally operated on a quarterly cadence—update the Gartner MQ analysis, refresh the battlecards, brief the sales team. That rhythm made sense when information moved slowly and manual synthesis was the only option. It makes less sense when AI agents can track pricing changes, sentiment shifts, hiring patterns, and product launches continuously, synthesizing competitive signals in real time rather than retrospectively.

Unit 3 introduced this shift, and the BattleCoach demonstration at last week's Office Hours illustrated what it looks like in practice—battle briefs generated on demand, objection handling in context, competitive scenarios simulated before the customer call rather than analyzed after it.

4. Enablement When Execution Speed Commoditizes

There's a question that few sales enablement teams have fully confronted: what happens when every company's reps have AI assistants capable of generating pitch decks in seconds, summarizing call notes automatically, and suggesting next steps based on deal patterns? If everyone has access to that acceleration, execution speed stops being a differentiator. The competitive moat moves upstream—to the quality of the positioning, the specificity of the use cases, the depth of the competitive insight that feeds those AI systems.

Unit 5 explored this dynamic. The insight is that battlecards, personas, and messaging frameworks aren't just sales enablement assets anymore; they're the training data for your company's AI-powered selling motion. The quality of those inputs determines the quality of the AI outputs, which means PMM work becomes more consequential, not less, as automation expands.

5. Workflow Architecture as a Core Skill

Every lab in this curriculum involved working alongside AI tools—the Competitive Analyzer, the Persona Builder, the PMM Assistant. These weren't tutorials in the traditional sense; they were simulations of workflow patterns that will become routine as agent capabilities embed into standard enterprise tools.

The meta-skill that emerges isn't prompt engineering. It's workflow architecture: how to structure a process so that AI handles the repeatable elements while human judgment focuses on strategy and exceptions; how to review AI outputs without becoming a bottleneck; how to maintain quality standards when automation handles 80% of the execution. These are questions that will define PMM effectiveness over the next several years, and the curriculum has provided a space to practice answers.

What Comes Next

The Gartner forecast—33% by 2028—functions as a kind of permission structure. It gives executives cover to invest, vendors cover to build, and practitioners cover to experiment. But the actual timeline appears to be compressing. Salesforce has Agentforce in market. HubSpot launched Agent Hub. ServiceNow, Microsoft, and SAP are all shipping agentic capabilities now, not in two years.

The PMMs who navigate this transition effectively won't necessarily be the ones who "learned AI" in the narrow sense. They'll be the ones who learned to work in systems where AI is ambient—present in every tool, embedded in every workflow, influencing every decision. The curriculum has been building that capability, unit by unit, even when the connection to agentic futures wasn't explicit.

Units 11 and 12 will continue in that direction. But the foundation is in place.
